phonemes.desc: The s is voiceless, the u as in “put”; the r is trilled.
Final r is sounded — “SOOR-tr”. The name means “the black one”, from the noun svart “black”.
The anglicised “Surt” drops the final r; the canonical Old Norse form keeps it.

kin.label: Anglicised
kin.form: Surt — the dropped-final form, kept as a separate lexicon entry

kin.label: Attestation
kin.form: Poetic Edda (Völuspá, Vafþrúðnismál) and Snorri’s Edda

pronunciation.note: The name is the adjective “black” nominalised — the fire-giant is the black one at the world’s end.

domains.title: The Black One, the Fire at the End
domains.subtitle: The Fire-Giant of Múspellsheimr
domains.lead: Surtr is the fire that ends the world: the black giant of Múspellsheimr, the realm of flame beyond the world’s rim, who will ride forth at Ragnarök with his burning sword brighter than the sun, defeat Freyr, and set the nine worlds ablaze — from whose surge the renewed earth rises. The Völuspá gives him the last word of the old world and the first light of the new.

cards.name: The Burning Sword
cards.desc: His sword shines brighter than the sun; with it he splits the world-tree’s shelter and sets the sky afire.

cards.name: Múspellsheimr
cards.desc: His realm of fire, the southernmost of the nine worlds — hot and radiant, guarded for the last battle.

cards.name: The Doom of Freyr
cards.desc: At Ragnarök he kills Freyr, who lacks his own sword — the gods’ summer falls to the world’s fire.

cards.name: The Renewer
cards.desc: From his fire the new earth rises green — the destroyer as the price of the world’s rebirth.

mythology.lead: Surtr’s mythology is the eschaton itself: he barely acts in the world’s story because his role is to end it. The Eddic poems give him Múspellsheimr, the sword of the sun’s brightness, the march at Ragnarök, the killing of Freyr, and the fire that consumes and renews. He is the Norse pantheon’s only fire-god — the flames of the end, kept outside the world until the world’s last hour.

myths.title: The One from the South
myths.text: The seeress’ prophecy reserves its starkest stanzas for him: ‘Surtr comes from the south with the bane of branches, the sun of the battle-gods shone from his sword.’ He rides first of the doom-forces; his arrival is the sign that the last battle has begun, and the sky itself catches fire from his blade.

myths.title: The Contest of Wisdom
myths.text: Odin’s wisdom-contest with the giant Vafþrúðnir fixes the cosmography: Surtr and the Æsir’s gods will meet at the field of Vígríðr, and ‘he will return home victorious’ from the encounter with Freyr. The poem’s calm arithmetic of doom — the lists of who kills whom — gives Surtr the war’s decisive duel.

myths.title: The Guardian of the Flame-Realm
myths.text: Snorri’s prose Edda places him as Múspellsheimr’s guardian from the beginning — the fire that predates the world and will outlast it. His sons, the ‘sons of Múspell’, ride with him; their host waits at the world’s rim through every age, kept out by the world’s green and the gods’ vigil.

myths.title: The Fire That Renews
myths.text: The Norse end is not the Christian end: after Surtr’s fire the earth rises green from the sea, the gods’ survivors meet, and the world begins again. The fire-giant’s destruction is the renewal’s price — the black one’s blaze is the last act of the old world and the first condition of the new.

lore.syncretism: Surtr is the Norse eschaton’s Persian fire: comparatists long ago paired him with the Zoroastrian world-fire and the volcanic destroyers of other traditions; and his role — the outsider-god of flame who ends and purifies — reads like a structural cousin of the Vedic Agni pushed to the world’s edge. Wagner’s Loge and Tolkien’s surtur-imagery carried him into modern fantasy as the type of the world-ending fire.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Völuspá’s ‘sun of the battle-gods’ image remains Norse mythology’s most quoted line of doom; and Surtr is the fantasy genre’s template for the fire-giant — from D&D’s fire giants to video games, his name is the standard label for volcanic end-bosses. Iceland’s volcanic place-names (Surtshellir, the ‘cave of Surtr’) keep him in the landscape itself.
lore.extendedMeditation: Surtr: the black one, restored in plain letters that hold no fire and yet smoulder. The lexicon keeps the full Old Norse form — the trilled r, the dropped-nothing spelling — because a world-ending fire deserves an unabbreviated name.

sources.name: Snorri, Gylfaginning (Múspellsheimr and the sons of Múspell)

lore.archaeology: Surtr’s monuments are volcanic: Iceland’s Surtshellir cave was used from the settlement age, its name the giant’s. The Eddic manuscripts — Codex Regius and its kin — give the words; the island’s lava-fields give the theatre.
lore.cult: No cult of Surtr is recorded — one does not worship the end. But the volcanic placenames and the Völuspá’s recitation tradition keep his name in the North’s mouth; and the modern Ásatrú movement’s Ragnarök-rites address the fire he brings.
lore.iconography: A giant wreathed in flame, sword raised like a second sun; black against his own fire — the svart one made visible by his blaze. His icon is the burning sword held high at the world’s rim.
lore.reception: Comparative eschatology sets him beside the world-fires of Persia and the volcano-gods of the Pacific as the destroyer whose blaze renews; and modern fantasy made his name generic — ‘Surt’ appears in more games and novels than any other Eddic name. The black one has become the genre’s default apocalypse.
